comments.author: mdrxy
comments.body:
Thanks for the clear repro. One question before we prioritize this: what real user path is calling `llm.generate(...)` directly here?

`generate()` is still part of the lower-level chat model API, and we should avoid crashing there, but it is not an API surface we actively promote for typical user code anymore. The recommended paths are generally `invoke()`, `ainvoke()`, `stream()`, `astream()`, `batch()`, or `abatch()`.

The important distinction is that default `batch()` runs multiple `invoke()` calls, so it usually does not hit this combine path. The failure here requires `generate()`/`agenerate()` with multiple message lists, where LangChain combines multiple `llm_output` dictionaries:

```python
llm.generate([
    [HumanMessage(content="a")],
    [HumanMessage(content="b")],
])
```

Can you share where this pattern is coming from in practice? For example:

- direct application code calling `llm.generate(...)`
- an older chain/agent abstraction
- a callback/tracing/evaluation path
- migration from older LangChain APIs
- another library wrapping LangChain models

That context would help us understand whether this is mostly a defensive compatibility fix for a lower-level method, or whether there is a higher-level promoted path that is unexpectedly reaching `generate()` with multiple prompts.

comments.author: abcgco
comments.body:
Honest answer first: I found this by auditing the partner packages for this merge pattern after #38482 (same failure, mistralai) was filed — so no first-party production stack trace from me. Mapping to your list, the paths that reach `generate()`/`agenerate()` with multiple message lists without anyone writing `llm.generate(...)`:

**Older chain abstractions:** `LLMChain` — deprecated since 0.1.17 (removal slated for 2.0) but still shipped in `langchain-classic` 1.0.8 — packs the whole `input_list` into a single `generate_prompt(...)` call in `generate()` ([source](https://github.com/langchain-ai/langchain/blob/master/libs/langchain/langchain_classic/chains/llm.py#L120-L134)), with `apply()` built on it (docstring: "Utilize the LLM generate method for speed gains"). `MapReduceDocumentsChain.combine_docs()` runs `llm_chain.apply(...)` across all mapped documents ([source](https://github.com/langchain-ai/langchain/blob/master/libs/langchain/langchain_classic/chains/combine_documents/map_reduce.py#L236)), so classic map-reduce summarization/QA combines one `llm_output` per document on every run.

**Libraries wrapping LangChain models:** ragas routes judge calls through `generate_prompt`/`agenerate_prompt`, and its fallback for models without native `n` support packs `prompts=[prompt] * n` into one call ([source](https://github.com/explodinggradients/ragas/blob/main/src/ragas/llms/base.py#L251-L255)).

On "why now": this path had been stable — it only started crashing once providers began returning nested `*_tokens_details` blocks in `usage` (the issue links a live Fireworks payload with `prompt_tokens_details.cached_tokens`), so existing code regressed without any user-side change. And at least one other user independently filed the same failure on mistralai (#38482).

Agreed on the `batch()` distinction — default `batch()` fans out over `invoke()`, so `_combine_llm_outputs` only ever sees a single `llm_output` on that path and the merge never happens. The failure needs the `generate()`/`agenerate()` + N-prompts surface.

So to answer your framing directly: this is a defensive compatibility fix for a lower-level surface — the callers I can point to are deprecated-but-shipped classic chains, migration-era code, and eval wrappers — and the failure mode is a crash rather than a wrong number. The fix mirrors `langchain-openai`'s `_update_token_usage` one-for-one; #38646 has it ready with parametrized regression tests.

github.title: ChatAnthropic streaming drops thinking field from empty thinking blocks (signature_delta-only), replay fails with 400 thinking.thinking: Field required
github.author: Seo-yul

comments.author: anneheartrecord
comments.body:
Ran into this in an agent loop too. Happy to send a PR if you can assign me.

The empty-block case is what's missing. For a normal thinking block the `thinking` key comes from the `thinking_delta`, so reconstructing the block from the deltas works. But for an empty adaptive-thinking block there's no `thinking_delta` at all — just `content_block_start` (thinking="") and a `signature_delta` — and `content_block_start` is intentionally dropped when both `thinking` and `signature` are empty (matching the text-block behavior, `test_empty_thinking_content_block_start_emits_no_chunk`). So the block ends up reconstructed from the `signature_delta` alone, which has no `thinking` key, and replay hits `400 thinking.thinking: Field required`.

Rather than emitting the empty start (which would break the text/thinking symmetry), the smaller fix is in the `signature_delta` branch of `_make_message_chunk_from_anthropic_event`: default `thinking` to `""` when building the block from a signature delta, so the reconstructed block always carries the field:

```python
elif event.delta.type in {"thinking_delta", "signature_delta"}:
    content_block = event.delta.model_dump()
    content_block["index"] = event.index
    content_block["type"] = "thinking"
    if event.delta.type == "signature_delta":
        content_block.setdefault("thinking", "")
    message_chunk = AIMessageChunk(content=[content_block])
```

For a normal block the `thinking_delta` still supplies the real text and the empty string from the signature delta just concatenates away, so nothing changes there. Branch with the fix + a unit test built on your repro (aggregate the events, then `_get_request_payload` to confirm the replayed block validates):

https://github.com/anneheartrecord/langchain/tree/fix/anthropic-empty-thinking-block

comments.author: Madhav-000-s
comments.body:
Hi, I'd like to work on this — I've verified the root cause on current master and have a minimal fix in mind.

Root cause

Two things combine in _make_message_chunk_from_anthropic_event (libs/partners/anthropic/langchain_anthropic/chat_models.py):

content_block_start events only emit a chunk for tool_use / tool_result / document / redacted_thinking blocks. For a thinking block, the start event (which carries thinking="") is dropped, so the block is reconstructed entirely from subsequent deltas.
The signature_delta branch builds its content block from event.delta.model_dump(), which contains only signature — no thinking key.
For a normal thinking block this works, because the thinking key is supplied by the thinking_delta chunks. But an empty adaptive-thinking block streams content_block_start (dropped) followed by only a signature_delta, so the aggregated message ends up with {"type": "thinking", "signature": ..., "index": 0} — the required thinking field is missing. Replaying that message to the API then fails with 400 thinking.thinking: Field required, exactly as described above.

Proposed fix

In the signature_delta branch, include "thinking": "" in the emitted content block:

Empty blocks: the signature chunk alone now aggregates to a valid {"type": "thinking", "thinking": "", "signature": ...} block that round-trips to the API.
Non-empty blocks: chunk merging concatenates string values, so the trailing "" is a no-op on the text already accumulated from thinking_delta chunks — no behavior change for the normal path.
One-line change, no public API surface touched.

Test plan

Unit tests in tests/unit_tests/test_chat_models.py (no network): replay the deterministic event sequence from this issue (content_block_start with empty thinking, then signature_delta only) and assert the aggregated block contains thinking; plus a companion test for a normal thinking-block sequence (thinking_deltas + signature_delta) asserting the thinking text is unchanged, to guard against regressions in the non-empty path.

Could a maintainer assign this to me? I'll open the PR right away once assigned.

comments.author: bolexyro
comments.body:
The 400 error here isn’t about using both config and context, it’s specifically about using both configurable and context together.

In other words, this line in the error:

`Cannot specify both configurable and context.
`

refers to the configurable field inside config, not the entire config argument.

✅ You can safely pass both config and context as long as config doesn’t contain a configurable key.

So, instead of doing this:

```
config = {"configurable": {"thread_id": thread_id}}
context = {"user_id": "123"}

```

You can move those fields up into your context:

`context = {"user_id": "123", "thread_id": thread_id}
`

and omit the configurable block entirely.

However, with this approach, checkpointing still doesn’t work, since the checkpointer only looks for thread_id inside config["configurable"], not in context.

I’m currently working on a fix for that so checkpointing continues to work seamlessly when using only context.

comments.author: Solaris-star
comments.body:
I dug into this and have a fix ready (was in #39103 before the auto-close).

**Root cause:** In `_format_messages` (chat_models.py), a `SystemMessage` built from `content_blocks` forwards each dict block verbatim:

```python
system = [
    (block if isinstance(block, dict) else {"type": "text", "text": block})
    for block in message.content
]
```

`create_text_block()` mints an `id` (e.g. `"lc_<uuid4>"`) on the block, and that `id` reaches Anthropic's `system` parameter, which rejects it with `system.0.id: Extra inputs are not permitted`.

**Proposed fix:** Allowlist the keys Anthropic accepts on a system text block — `type`, `text`, `cache_control`, `citations` — which is exactly the allowlist already used for text blocks in regular message content (chat_models.py:600-617). This drops the `id` while preserving `cache_control` and `citations`.

I have this implemented with two unit tests (id stripped from a `create_text_block()` system block; `cache_control` preserved), both failing on the unfixed code and passing with the fix, and the full `test_chat_models.py` suite (148 tests) green. Happy to reopen the PR once assigned. Would this approach be acceptable?

github.title: [Bug]: Bedrock Converse streaming produces string `tool_kwargs` in `ToolCallBlock` instead of dict
github.author: jimhotchkin-wf

comments.author: dosubot[bot]
comments.body:
<!-- Greeting -->
Hi @jimhotchkin-wf! I'm [Dosu](https://go.dosu.dev/dosubot) and I’m helping the llama_index team.

<!-- Answer -->
Thanks for the detailed bug report. I investigated the current state of the code and have some observations:

**The core issue is real, but the details differ from the report.** The current `base.py` has 773 lines total [[1]](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/blob/ddeb22219e1255829d07cde44e172c8f8c6bd2ff/llama-index-integrations/llms/llama-index-llms-bedrock-converse/llama_index/llms/bedrock_converse/base.py), not the ~978+ implied by the report. Also, `ToolCallBlock` does not exist in the LlamaIndex codebase — tool calls are stored as raw dicts in `ChatMessage.additional_kwargs["tool_calls"]`, and the class used downstream is `ToolSelection`.

**What actually happens in streaming:** The streaming code paths (`stream_chat` and `astream_chat`) accumulate the `"input"` field as a concatenated JSON string [[2]](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/blob/ddeb22219e1255829d07cde44e172c8f8c6bd2ff/llama-index-integrations/llms/llama-index-llms-bedrock-converse/llama_index/llms/bedrock_converse/base.py#L434-L440) [[3]](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/blob/ddeb22219e1255829d07cde44e172c8f8c6bd2ff/llama-index-integrations/llms/llama-index-llms-bedrock-converse/llama_index/llms/bedrock_converse/base.py#L594-L600) and yield `ChatResponse` objects with those raw dicts (containing string `"input"`) in `additional_kwargs["tool_calls"]`.

**The `get_tool_calls_from_response` method already handles this correctly** — it checks `isinstance(tool_call["input"], str)` and parses it via `parse_partial_json()` before constructing `ToolSelection` objects with a proper dict `tool_kwargs` [[4]](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/blob/ddeb22219e1255829d07cde44e172c8f8c6bd2ff/llama-index-integrations/llms/llama-index-llms-bedrock-converse/llama_index/llms/bedrock_converse/base.py#L733-L744).

**So the Bedrock Converse adapter itself works end-to-end** because the agent workflow calls `get_tool_calls_from_response()` which normalizes the string. However, the broader concern is valid: if another provider's adapter consumes the raw `additional_kwargs["tool_calls"]` dicts from a Bedrock streaming session (e.g., when persisting and replaying chat history cross-provider), it would encounter string `"input"` values instead of dicts.

**Suggested fix location:** Parsing `current_tool_call["input"]` from string to dict at the `contentBlockStop` event (when the tool use block is complete) would be the cleanest approach. This normalizes the data at the source so all downstream consumers — whether Bedrock's own `get_tool_calls_from_response` or another provider — see a dict. This is a one-line addition per streaming method rather than touching 6 construction sites.

github.title: [Bug]: to_openai_message_dict doesn't JSON-serialize ToolCallBlock.tool_kwargs and breaks cross-provider agent workflows
github.author: saadshaikh3

comments.author: dosubot[bot]
comments.body:
<!-- Answer -->
Thanks for the detailed bug report. The arguments serialization issue you've identified is real, but it's actually part of a **broader cross-provider tool call format incompatibility** in LlamaIndex.

When AgentWorkflow hands off between agents, all agents share a single `ChatMemoryBuffer` with no message transformation during handoffs [[1]](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/blob/ddeb22219e1255829d07cde44e172c8f8c6bd2ff/llama-index-core/llama_index/core/agent/workflow/multi_agent_workflow.py#L488-L493). The `to_openai_message_dict` function then does a raw `message_dict.update(message.additional_kwargs)` [[2]](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/blob/ddeb22219e1255829d07cde44e172c8f8c6bd2ff/llama-index-integrations/llms/llama-index-llms-openai/llama_index/llms/openai/utils.py#L427), which directly merges whatever provider-specific metadata exists — including Anthropic-formatted tool calls — into the OpenAI message dict.

The problem goes deeper than just `arguments` not being JSON-serialized. Anthropic stores tool calls in a completely different format than OpenAI expects [[3]](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/issues/19898):

- **Anthropic**: `{"input": {...}, "name": "...", "type": "tool_use", "id": "..."}`
- **OpenAI**: `{"type": "function", "function": {"name": "...", "arguments": "<json string>"}, "id": "..."}`

So even with the `json.dumps()` fix, Anthropic-originated tool calls would still fail when passed to OpenAI because the key names and structure don't match. This is a [known systemic issue](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/issues/19898) — a maintainer has acknowledged it and suggested a unified tool call data structure, though it hasn't been implemented yet.

That said, your suggested fix is still a good incremental improvement for cases where tool calls happen to already be in OpenAI format (e.g., when the same OpenAI provider is used across turns). The `to_openai_responses_message_dict` path already applies this serialization [[4]](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/blob/ddeb22219e1255829d07cde44e172c8f8c6bd2ff/llama-index-integrations/llms/llama-index-llms-openai/llama_index/llms/openai/utils.py#L522-L531), so applying it in `to_openai_message_dict` as well would improve consistency.

A related issue (#21124) also tracks [multiple serialization bugs](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/issues/21124) in these utility functions, including this same `tool_kwargs` serialization gap.

github.title: calling `model_dump()` on pydantic state variables drops `tool_calls` in AIMessage
github.author: Thommy257

comments.author: ahmedibrahimX
comments.body:
Hi! I'd like to help with this issue. I've investigated the root cause and have a proposed solution I'd like to run by you before implementing.

## Root Cause
The issue occurs during Pydantic serialization. When `State.model_dump()` is called on a model with `list[BaseMessage]` type annotations, Pydantic treats this as a union and serializes each message using only the `BaseMessage` schema, which drops subclass-specific fields like `tool_calls`.

**Why the behavior differs:**
- `AIMessage.model_dump()` → uses concrete `AIMessage` schema → all fields preserved
- `State(messages=[msg]).model_dump()` → uses base `BaseMessage` schema → subclass fields lost

## Proposed Solution
Modify `JsonPlusSerializer` in `langgraph/checkpoint/serde/jsonplus.py` to handle `BaseMessage` objects specially:

1. **In `_msgpack_default()`**: Check for `BaseMessage` instances before the general Pydantic model check and serialize using the concrete message class
2. **In `_msgpack_ext_hook()`**: Use `LC_REVIVER` during deserialization to properly reconstruct message objects with all fields

**Benefits:**
- [x] Fixes the issue without requiring changes to user code
- [x] Preserves backward compatibility  
- [x] Graceful fallback if `langchain_core` isn't available
- [x] Works for any State schema with message lists

Would this approach work for you? Happy to share a draft PR or adjust based on your feedback!

comments.author: ahmedibrahimX
comments.body: I've implemented this solution in PR #6685. The fix adds special handling for BaseMessage objects in both standalone and nested contexts (within Pydantic State objects). All tests passing and ready for review!

comments.author: ahmedibrahimX
comments.body:
Hi @Thommy257,

I did a deep investigation into this issue and wanted to share what I found.

### The Good News

LangGraph’s checkpoint system already handles this correctly, `tool_calls` are preserved when using MemorySaver and other checkpoint savers. I tested this with State defined as both a TypedDict and a Pydantic BaseModel, and both work as expected.

### What’s Causing the Behavior

The issue you’re seeing happens when `state.model_dump()` is called directly inside the node:

```python
def agent_node(state: State) -> State:
    msg = agent.invoke(state.model_dump())
    return State(messages=[msg])
```

When Pydantic serializes a model containing `list[BaseMessage]`, it uses the base class schema, which doesn’t include subclass-specific fields like tool_calls. This is expected Pydantic behavior and occurs outside LangGraph’s serialization path.

### Recommended Pattern
Instead of calling `model_dump()` on the full state, let LangGraph pass message objects through directly:

```python
def agent_node(state: State) -> State:
    msg = agent.invoke({"messages": state.messages})
    return State(messages=[msg])
```
This preserves message types and tool_calls.

### Why This Happens
LangGraph’s checkpoint persistence uses JsonPlusSerializer, which has special handling to preserve message subclasses. Calling `model_dump()` directly skips that mechanism and relies purely on Pydantic’s base-class serialization.

### PR Status

I opened PR #6685 initially, but closed it after realizing it addressed a different edge case (nested Pydantic data in custom checkpoint payloads). This issue is best solved through usage rather than a code change.

Hope this helps — happy to clarify or test further.

comments.author: Thommy257
comments.body:
Hi @ahmedibrahimX,

Thanks for your response. In my specific use case, `State` has numerous variables that I would potentially like to pass to the agent. I have to admit that I'm a bit lazy here, but keeping track of what variables need to be passed to the ChatPromptTemplate and which not seems a bit tedious.

I solved the issue by adding a `shallow_dump` method to my `State` class:

```python
def shallow_dump(self, /) -> dict[str, Any]:
    """Get a shallow dictionary dump of the model, depth 1 only."""
    keys = chain(self.__class__.model_fields.keys(),
                 self.__class__.model_computed_fields.keys())
    return {k: getattr(self, k) for k in keys}
```

github.title: [Bug]: Ollama does not respect the client's initialization
github.author: josx

comments.author: dosubot[bot]
comments.body:
<!-- Answer -->
You've found a confirmed bug! The issue is in the [client property implementation](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/blob/ddeb22219e1255829d07cde44e172c8f8c6bd2ff/llama-index-integrations/llms/llama-index-llms-ollama/llama_index/llms/ollama/base.py#L185-L196) - while the `__init__` method accepts and stores your custom `async_client`, the properties always create **new** clients:

```python
@property
def client(self) -> Client:
    if self._client is None:
        self._client = Client(host=self.base_url, timeout=self.request_timeout)
    return self._client
```

The problem: you're passing an `AsyncClient`, but you're calling `llm.complete()` (sync), which uses `self.client` (the sync client property). Since you didn't pass a sync `client`, `self._client` is `None`, so it creates a new one without your headers.

Even if you used async methods, there's still a catch: `get_context_window()` is called during `_model_kwargs` and it uses `self.client.show()` - triggering the sync client creation before your async client would ever be used.

**Workaround**: Pass the **sync** `Client` with your headers:

```python
from llama_index.llms.ollama import Ollama
from ollama import Client

client = Client(host=host, headers={"Authorization": "Bearer MY_API_KEY"})
llm = Ollama(client=client, base_url=host, model=model)
```

This should work because if `self._client` is not `None`, it returns your client instead of creating a new one.

github.author: JNassar77

comments.author: JNassar77
comments.body:
We found a workaround that fixes the issue completely.

Root cause: The action string contains literal newline characters (chr(10)) 
inside the JSON string value. These are not valid in JSON strings, so 
json.loads() fails with "Expecting ',' delimiter".

Fix applied in browser_use/llm/anthropic/chat.py, before model_validate():

    if isinstance(_input, dict) and 'action' in _input and isinstance(_input['action'], str):
        action_str = _input['action']
        _parsed = False
        # Stage 1: standard json.loads
        try:
            _input['action'] = json.loads(action_str)
            _parsed = True
        except (json.JSONDecodeError, TypeError):
            pass
        # Stage 2: escape literal control chars
        if not _parsed:
            try:
                _BS = chr(92)
                cleaned = action_str
                cleaned = cleaned.replace(chr(10), _BS + 'n')
                cleaned = cleaned.replace(chr(13), _BS + 'r')
                cleaned = cleaned.replace(chr(9),  _BS + 't')
                _input['action'] = json.loads(cleaned)
                _parsed = True
            except (json.JSONDecodeError, TypeError):
                pass
        # Stage 3: synthetic done action as last resort
        if not _parsed:
            import re as _re
            _m = _re.search(r'"done"\s*:\s*\{\s*"text"\s*:\s*"(.+)', action_str, _re.DOTALL)
            raw_text = _m.group(1).rstrip('}' + chr(34) + ' ' + chr(9) + chr(10) + chr(13)) if _m else action_str
            _input['action'] = [{'done': {'text': raw_text}}]

After this fix: agent completes successfully, done action returns full result.

1. the helper binds/listens on port `0`
2. uvicorn receives that already-bound socket

This looks worth pinning down as a protocol-level regression rather than only an implementation bug.

For `flaky streamable HTTP/SSE tests TOCTOU port race`, the acceptance test I would want is a minimal client/server fixture that records the exact JSON-RPC or HTTP exchange, then asserts both the wire result and the local lifecycle state after the failure path. In MCP deployments, the dangerous failures are often not just wrong return values; they are pending requests, dropped notifications, mismatched session state, or errors that get translated into a generic response and become impossible to diagnose.

A useful fix boundary would preserve three signals: the protocol error sent to the peer, the local exception or cancellation reason available to application code, and a trace/log field that ties the two together. That makes the behavior debuggable for agent hosts without requiring every host to special-case this SDK detail.

github.title: Chroma vector store silently downgrades unknown filter operators to equality
github.author: HrushiYadav

comments.author: kartik-mem0
comments.body:
Thanks for the report and the clean repro one-liner.

## Triage Notes

**What we've established:**
- `ChromaDB._generate_where_clause`'s inner `convert_condition` (`mem0/vector_stores/chroma.py:267-301`) maps known operators (`eq`/`ne`/`gt`/`gte`/`lt`/`lte`/`in`/`nin`/`contains`/`icontains`) to Chroma's `$`-prefixed equivalents; anything else falls into the `else` branch at lines 295-297 and is silently rewritten to `{"$eq": val}` — so `{"age": {"betwen": [10, 20]}}` quietly becomes `{"age": {"$eq": [10, 20]}}` with no error or warning.
- This is a real inconsistency between backends, not just a hypothetical: Qdrant's filter handling (`mem0/vector_stores/qdrant.py:332-335`) raises `ValueError("Unsupported filter operator(s) for field ...")` for the same class of input, so Chroma is the outlier that fails silently instead of fast.
- Because this covers any operator the shared filter DSL doesn't explicitly enumerate for Chroma, it's also a forward-compatibility trap: a new operator added elsewhere to the filter surface (or a simple typo) would silently misfilter on Chroma specifically, with nothing flagging it.

**Reproduction:** Confirmed — `ChromaDB._generate_where_clause({"age": {"betwen": [10, 20]}})` on current `main` returns `{"age": {"$eq": [10, 20]}}` exactly as reported.

**Root cause:** The `else` branch of `convert_condition` in `_generate_where_clause` (`mem0/vector_stores/chroma.py:295-297`) silently downgrades any unrecognized filter operator to equality instead of raising.

**Severity:** P1. It's a silent wrong-result bug — `search()`/`list()` calls with a malformed or unsupported operator return incorrect results with zero signal to the caller, in a widely-used self-hosted vector store backend, and it's a live footgun against future filter-DSL additions.

**Next step:** PR #6259 is open against this issue.

comments.author: tokoyoda
comments.body:
I hit what appears to be the same `ClosedResourceError` on mcp 1.26.0 with streamable-http transport (stateful mode). The crash occurs reliably whenever the MCP client disconnects while a long-running tool handler is still in progress. Below is a minimal reproduction and root cause analysis.

### Reproduction

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
# /// script
# requires-python = "==3.14.*"
# dependencies = ["mcp==1.26.0", "httpx==0.28.1"]
# ///
"""
Reproduce ClosedResourceError when DELETE is sent during in-flight tool handler.

    uv run reproduce_minimal.py

https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/python-sdk/issues/1967
"""

import asyncio
import httpx
from mcp.server import FastMCP

# ---------- Server ----------

server = FastMCP("repro-server", host="localhost", port=9999)


@server.tool(description="Simulates a long-running operation")
async def slow_task(seconds: float = 3.0) -> dict:
    print(f"[server] slow_task: sleeping {seconds}s ...")
    await asyncio.sleep(seconds)
    print("[server] slow_task: done, sending response ...")
    return {"ok": True}


# ---------- Client ----------

BASE = "http://localhost:9999/mcp"
H = {"Accept": "application/json, text/event-stream", "Content-Type": "application/json"}


async def run_client():
    """Init session -> call slow_task -> DELETE mid-flight -> observe crash."""
    await asyncio.sleep(2)  # wait for server startup

    async with httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=30) as c:
        # 1. Initialize
        r = await c.post(BASE, json={
            "jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 1, "method": "initialize",
            "params": {
                "protocolVersion": "2024-11-05",
                "capabilities": {},
                "clientInfo": {"name": "repro", "version": "0.1"},
            },
        }, headers=H)
        sid = r.headers["mcp-session-id"]
        print(f"[client] session: {sid[:12]}...")
        sh = {**H, "mcp-session-id": sid}

        # 2. Initialized notification
        await c.post(BASE, json={"jsonrpc": "2.0", "method": "notifications/initialized"}, headers=sh)

    # 3. Call slow_task (fire-and-forget with short timeout)
    async def call_slow():
        async with httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=httpx.Timeout(1.0)) as c:
            try:
                await c.post(BASE, json={
                    "jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 2, "method": "tools/call",
                    "params": {"name": "slow_task", "arguments": {"seconds": 3}},
                }, headers=sh)
            except httpx.ReadTimeout:
                pass  # expected

    asyncio.create_task(call_slow())
    await asyncio.sleep(1)  # let task start on server

    # 4. DELETE -> terminate session while slow_task is still running
    print("[client] sending DELETE to terminate session mid-task ...")
    async with httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=5) as c:
        r = await c.delete(BASE, headers=sh)
        print(f"[client] DELETE response: {r.status_code}")

    # 5. Wait for server to hit the error
    print("[client] waiting for slow_task to finish on server ...")
    await asyncio.sleep(3)
    print("[client] done")


# ---------- Main ----------

async def main():
    import threading
    t = threading.Thread(target=lambda: server.run(transport="streamable-http"), daemon=True)
    t.start()
    await run_client()

asyncio.run(main())
```

### Root Cause

`terminate()` closes `_write_stream` immediately without waiting for in-flight handlers. When a handler finishes and calls `respond()` → `_send_response()` → `_write_stream.send()`, it raises `ClosedResourceError` which propagates unhandled through the `TaskGroup`, crashing the session.

1. Client sends **DELETE** → [`_handle_delete_request`](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/python-sdk/blob/v1.26.0/src/mcp/server/streamable_http.py#L497) → [`terminate()`](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/python-sdk/blob/v1.26.0/src/mcp/server/streamable_http.py#L513) closes all streams
2. [`_receive_loop()`](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/python-sdk/blob/v1.26.0/src/mcp/shared/session.py#L250) exits its `async with` block → `_write_stream` closed
3. [`Server.run()`](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/python-sdk/blob/v1.26.0/src/mcp/server/lowlevel/server.py#L575) `TaskGroup` waits for in-flight handlers
4. Handler calls [`message.respond()`](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/python-sdk/blob/v1.26.0/src/mcp/server/lowlevel/server.py#L693) → [`_send_response()`](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/python-sdk/blob/v1.26.0/src/mcp/shared/session.py#L226) → `_write_stream.send()` → **`ClosedResourceError`**

The existing [`ClosedResourceError` catch](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/python-sdk/blob/v1.26.0/src/mcp/shared/session.py#L323) in `_receive_loop` only guards the **read** side, not the write path used by handlers.

Note: [`streamablehttp_client`](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/python-sdk/blob/v1.26.0/src/mcp/client/streamable_http.py#L346) defaults to `terminate_on_close=True`, so every normal client disconnect sends DELETE — meaning any long-running tool handler will crash the session.

comments.author: qflen

Reproduced on `master` (6f7c8f54) with `pydantic==2.14.0a1` on Python 3.13, same `TypeError: 'function' object is not subscriptable` while evaluating `'dict[str, Any] | None'`. I found two things: 1. The `_create_subset_model_v2` write is not the trigger. With `langchain-core` installed editable I commented out `rtn.__annotations__ = dict(selected_annotations)` (verified the edit was live with `inspect.getsource`) and the repro fails identically. That write does violate the `getattr`/`__dict__` invariant Viicos described in pydantic#13097, but fixing it alone won't resolve this issue. 2. The actual trigger is the definition of `AgentStatePydantic` in `langgraph.prebuilt.chat_agent_executor`, which `langchain.agents` reaches through `langchain.tools` (a re-export of `langgraph.prebuilt`). Statement-level bisection narrows it to the `remaining_steps: RemainingSteps = 25` field, where `RemainingSteps = Annotated[int, RemainingStepsManager]`. Defining any such model is enough, no `langchain.agents` needed: ```python # pydantic==2.14.0a1, langgraph 1.2.4 from langgraph.managed import RemainingSteps from pydantic import BaseModel class Poison(BaseModel): remaining_steps: RemainingSteps = 25 from langchain_core.language_models.llms import BaseLLM # TypeError ``` After `Poison` is defined, parametrizing `BaseLanguageModel[str]` produces a class with no `__annotations__` of its own in `__dict__`, while `getattr` returns the string annotations inherited from `BaseLanguageModel` (`language_models/base.py` uses `from __future__ import annotations`). During `BaseLLM` construction those strings get re-evaluated in a namespace where `BaseLLM`'s legacy `dict()` method shadows the builtin, hence the error. Without the trigger, the parametrized class gets its own `__annotations__` and nothing is re-evaluated. The divergence comes from pydantic's own parametrization path, not from anything writing `__annotations__`. Everything passes on stable pydantic (tested 2.12.5). What I haven't pinned down yet is why this metadata flips pydantic's parametrization behavior. Synthetic equivalents using my own `Annotated[int, GenericSubclass]` metadata don't reproduce, so some ingredient of `RemainingStepsManager` or `BaseLanguageModel` is still essential.
Verification commands (run from libs/langchain_v1) ```bash # original repro uv run --with "pydantic==2.14.0a1" python -c \ "import langchain.agents; from langchain_core.language_models.llms import BaseLLM" # minimal trigger, no langchain.agents uv run --with "pydantic==2.14.0a1" python -c " from langgraph.managed import RemainingSteps from pydantic import BaseModel class Poison(BaseModel): remaining_steps: RemainingSteps = 25 from langchain_core.language_models.llms import BaseLLM" # the import alone is fine uv run --with "pydantic==2.14.0a1" python -c \ "import langgraph.managed; from langchain_core.language_models.llms import BaseLLM; print('PASS')" # stable pydantic control uv run python -c \ "import langchain.agents; from langchain_core.language_models.llms import BaseLLM; print('PASS')" ``` Bisection: stubbed `langgraph.prebuilt.__init__` in `sys.modules` to isolate its four submodules (only `chat_agent_executor` triggers), exec'd its top-level statements incrementally (the crash starts at the `AgentStatePydantic` ClassDef), then ablated its two fields (`messages` passes, `remaining_steps` crashes).
My read is the primary defect is on the pydantic main side (2.14 is still alpha), and pydantic#13097 may be worth revisiting with this reduction since it was closed on the `__annotations__`-write theory. #### Plan: 1. Finish reducing to a pydantic-only repro and take it upstream, then coordinate where the real fix lands (pydantic, langgraph's `RemainingSteps` shape, or here). 2. Land the #34537-style `get_type_hints(..., include_extras=True)` cleanup in `_create_subset_model_v2` as hardening regardless (credit to @Aman071106's original PR), since the manual write does violate the invariant. 3. Add a regression test that runs on stable pydantic, plus whatever is preferred for prerelease coverage. @mdrxy could you assign me? Happy to adjust scope depending on how you want this split across repos.

github.title: [Bug]: Signature field not being provided in BedrockConverse requests (regression)
github.author: mattref

comments.author: dosubot[bot]
comments.body:
<!-- Answer -->
Your analysis is correct. The root cause is in [PR #20664](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/pull/20664)'s `extract_thinking_from_block()` function in `utils.py`, which only extracts the `text` field from `reasoningContent` and completely ignores the `signature` field:

```python
if "reasoningContent" in block:
    reasoning = block["reasoningContent"]
    if "reasoningText" in reasoning:
        return reasoning["reasoningText"].get("text")
    return reasoning.get("text")  # Only extracts text, ignores signature
```

When a streaming chunk contains only a signature (like `{"reasoningContent": {"signature": "...."}}`), this function returns `None`, causing the signature to be dropped. AWS Bedrock then rejects the incomplete thinking block with the ValidationException you're seeing.

This is a known issue area — [Issue #20349](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/issues/20349#issuecomment-3633482669) documents that `reasoningContent` blocks can contain a `signature` field that must be preserved for Bedrock's validation.

**Workaround**: As a temporary workaround, you can extract thinking content directly from raw event data: `event.raw['contentBlockDelta']['delta']['reasoningContent']['text']`.

**Required Fix**: The `extract_thinking_from_block()` function needs to be updated to handle both `text` and `signature` fields from `reasoningContent` to properly support extended thinking with tools.

<!-- Greeting -->
Hi @newtondotcom! I'm [Dosu](https://go.dosu.dev/dosubot) and I’m helping the llama_index team.

<!-- Answer -->
This is a known issue. The error occurs because `OpenAILike` inherits from the OpenAI base class, which [automatically sets `tool_choice` to `"required"` during structured prediction](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/blob/ddeb22219e1255829d07cde44e172c8f8c6bd2ff/llama-index-integrations/llms/llama-index-llms-openai/llama_index/llms/openai/base.py#L1040-L1041). However, since you set `is_function_calling_model=False`, your API endpoint doesn't support tools, causing the error.

**Workaround**: Explicitly pass `tool_choice="none"` when calling the structured LLM:

```python
sllm = client.as_structured_llm(Invoice)
response = sllm.complete(text, tool_choice="none")
```

**Alternative**: If your model actually supports function calling, set `is_function_calling_model=True` and `is_chat_model=True`:

```python
client = OpenAILike(
    base_url=os.getenv("BASE_URL"),
    api_key=os.getenv("API_KEY"),
    http_client=httpx.Client(verify=False),
    model="gpt-oss-20b",
    is_chat_model=True,
    is_function_calling_model=True
)
```

There's also a related fix in [PR #20740](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/pull/20740) that addresses `tool_choice` parameter forwarding through `FunctionCallingProgram`.

comments.author: thakoreh
comments.body:
## Root Cause Analysis

This error is **not caused by a missing dependency** in `pyproject.toml`. The `build-system.requires = ["hatchling"]` configuration is correct.

This is a known uv issue (astral-sh/uv#16228) caused by a **corrupted build cache**.

## Why the error is misleading

The error message suggests adding `hatchling.build` to `build-system.requires`, but `hatchling.build` is a **module path** (inside the `hatchling` package), not a PyPI package. Adding it would cause a different error.

## Solution

Clear the corrupted cache:

**For Podman:**
```bash
podman builder prune -a --external
```

If that doesn't work, reset the podman machine:
```bash
podman machine reset
```

**For Docker:**
```bash
docker builder prune -a
```

**Also try:**
```bash
uv cache clean
```

The build should succeed after clearing the cache. No code changes needed.

github.title: [bug] When a node relies on multiple input edges,  it will execute as soon as one of the edges meets the condition.
github.author: qq745639151

comments.author: le-codeur-rapide
comments.body:
Hi @qq745639151 , 
Langgraph creates **state graphs**, not dependency graphs. The way it works is that if you have an edge pointing from A to B, if A is executed during a step n, then B will be executed during step n+1, it does not mean that B needs A to be executed.

More specifically, **if there are 2 edges A1 -> B and A2 -> B, it does not mean that B needs A1 and A2 to be executed to run.** It means that if either A1 or A2 or executed during some step, B will be executed the next step.

If you want a node to run only if all nodes pointing to it have been executed, you can use the `defer=True` parameter of `.add_edge` method. [Documentation about defer](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/use-graph-api#defer-node-execution).

I hope this helps !

Thanks for the detailed and thoughtful report: much appreciated! 🤗

After reviewing the issue, I agree that supporting multiline function signatures is important and should definitely be addressed. However, regarding multiple decorators, I'm less certain. For a tool to be used in a remote Python executor, we need access to the full function body so it can be serialized and sent for execution. comments.author: HairlessVillager
comments.body:
😱

You have indeed pointed out a very serious issue. As far as I know, smolagents only sends the code of the function itself and some necessary `import` statements to the remote. It seems that smolagents has made an unrealistic assumption: utility functions will only depend on standard libraries or third-party libraries, and will not depend on custom classes, functions, or modules. If this assumption holds true, then sending code with decorators to the remote without sending the decorators themselves as dependencies is meaningless.

If that's the case, I can quickly think of two solutions:
1. Implement a more comprehensive dependency retrieval based on AST, and send the code, including the decorators, to the remote;
2. Explicitly prohibit the use of decorators in utility functions, for example, by throwing an exception.

I think we can first implement Solution 2, and then modify the `@tool` when the conditions for Solution 1 are met.

Is there any problem with my thinking? Do you have any ideas? Welcome to bring it up!

comments.author: albertvillanova
comments.body:

You're absolutely right: the current approach in smolagents assumes utility functions are self-contained. That assumption definitely breaks down when decorators introduce dependencies that aren’t captured in the function body. In that sense, sending code without decorators can lead to unpredictable or incorrect behavior.

I think your proposed solutions make a lot of sense. Implementing option 2 first (explicitly prohibiting decorators with a clear error message) would be a practical and safe stopgap. It can help avoid silent failures and clarify the current limitations.

Longer-term, I agree that option 1 is the ideal direction. A more robust dependency resolver could eventually allow us to serialize decorators (and their dependencies) along with the function body.

comments.author: albertvillanova
comments.body:
Hi @lvicentesanchez, thanks for reporting this!

The issue stems from how the `messages` content is formatted. By default, `smolagents.OpenAIServerModel` sends message content as an array of structured elements (e.g., `{"type": "text", "text": "..."}`), which is fully compliant with the OpenAI Chat Completions API spec: https://platform.openai.com/docs/api-reference/chat/create#chat-create-messages

However, not all providers implementing the OpenAI-compatible API support the full spec. In the case of **DeepInfra**, it appears that only `string`-type content is accepted (not arrays), which causes the 422 error when using `OpenAIServerModel`.

To work around this, you can pass `flatten_messages_as_text=True` to force `smolagents.OpenAIServerModel` to serialize message content to plain strings, which DeepInfra handles correctly.

You can check the `OpenAiServerModel` docs about `flatten_messages_as_text` here: https://huggingface.co/docs/smolagents/reference/models#smolagents.OpenAIServerModel.flatten_messages_as_text

comments.author: Chase-Xuu
comments.body:
I've identified and fixed this issue. PR incoming!

**Root Cause:**
The default downloads path was hardcoded to use `/tmp` (line 435 in profile.py):
```python
downloads_path = Path(f'/tmp/browser-use-downloads-{unique_id}')
```

On Windows, `/tmp` doesn't exist as a standard path. When Python's `pathlib.Path` interprets `/tmp` on Windows, it becomes something like `\tmp` under the current drive root, which typically doesn't exist and can't be created without admin privileges.

**Fix:**
Replaced the hardcoded `/tmp` with `tempfile.gettempdir()`, which returns the platform-appropriate temp directory:
- **Linux/Mac:** `/tmp`
- **Windows:** `C:\Users\<user>\AppData\Local\Temp` (or equivalent)

This is consistent with how `user_data_dir` is already handled (using `tempfile.mkdtemp()`).
